Backups and Disaster Recovery

1. Backups and Disaster Recovery

HarborWorks can rebuild a web server, but can it recover the correct content after deletion, corruption, or loss of its normal credentials? A backup strategy answers that question with a demonstrated restore. A successful copy command is useful evidence, but it is not the whole answer.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Chapter 21 — Backups and Disaster Recovery

2. A backup is proven through restore

Job completion, archive integrity and usable recovery are separate claims; prove recovery with a restore and acceptance test. A replica immediately copies an accidental deletion and has no recoverable earlier state.

SOURCE: A backup is proven through restore

3. Chapter 21 — Backups and Disaster Recovery

HarborWorks can rebuild a web server, but can it recover the correct content after deletion, corruption, or loss of its normal credentials? A backup strategy answers that question with a demonstrated restore. A successful copy command is useful evidence, but it is not the whole answer.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Chapter 21 — Backups and Disaster Recovery

4. 21.1 What Makes a Backup

A backup is a recoverable copy retained for specified failure scenarios and time periods. Define what it contains, when it represents the source, who can retrieve it, and which failures it survives. A second directory on the same disk does not survive loss of that disk. A replica that immediately repeats a deletion does not preserve the earlier state unless versioned recovery exists.

Separate three claims: the job completed, the stored data is intact, and the service can be restored. Job status supports the first. Integrity checking supports the second. An isolated restore and application test support the third. None should silently stand in for another.

A backup also contains operational dependencies: configuration, identity mappings, encryption keys, software versions, and instructions needed to interpret the data. Keep the keys and recovery documentation accessible under a failure model different from the server being protected.

Linux example — 21.1

Prove that a small archive restores its content.

What to check: cmp exits zero for matching bytes; keeping both copies locally is a demonstration, not an independent backup.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.1 What Makes a Backup

6. 21.2 Backup Strategies

Design from failure scenarios. Accidental deletion, a compromised administrator, a failed region, and an application bug require different retention and isolation boundaries. An attacker able to erase every copy with production credentials defeats an otherwise elaborate backup schedule.

For the small HarborStatus service, version-controlled configuration and reproducible packages reduce the amount of unique data. The approved status content, deployment metadata, and any locally created business state still need protection. Treat a Git repository as one component, not an automatic backup of ignored files, secrets, or uncommitted changes.

Choose frequency, retention, off-site location, immutability or offline protection where appropriate, encryption, and restore ownership together. A cheap storage tier with a long retrieval delay may satisfy archival needs while failing the service’s recovery target.

Linux example — 21.2

Inspect archive contents before restoring.

What to check: A checksum helps detect later change; it does not prove the original backup was complete.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.2 Backup Strategies

8. 21.3 Full, Incremental, and Differential Backups

A full backup captures the selected dataset. An incremental backup captures changes since the relevant preceding backup. A differential backup captures changes since the last full backup. Product terminology and internal implementation vary, so inspect the actual restore dependency chain.

In a simple file-backup model, a full plus several incrementals may save transfer time but require several sets for recovery. A full plus the latest differential has a different storage and restore tradeoff. Deduplicating tools may present synthetic full snapshots without physically copying every unchanged block each time.

Draw what must remain available to restore Thursday’s state. Then test loss of one component in the lab. The important fact is not which label the product uses; it is whether the required restore set is complete, verified, and available within the target time.

Linux example — 21.3

Create an incremental demonstration using a new workspace.

What to check: GNU tar's snapshot file tracks this chain; restore the full archive and increments in order in a disposable target.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.3 Full, Incremental, and Differential Backups

10. 21.4 RPO and RTO

The recovery point objective, or RPO, is the acceptable amount of data loss expressed as a time window. The recovery time objective, or RTO, is the target duration for restoring an agreed service level. Both are requirements selected by the business, not properties produced automatically by a backup tool.

Suppose HarborWorks chooses a teaching RPO of 24 hours and RTO of 60 minutes for its internal static site. A daily successful backup does not guarantee the RPO if two jobs fail unnoticed. A ten-minute file restore does not guarantee the RTO if finding credentials and rebuilding the host takes two hours.

Measure recovery from the defined start event to a verified usable service, including detection or approval time if the contract includes it. Record assumptions explicitly. The numbers above are illustrative exercise targets, not claims that they suit another workload.

Linux example — 21.4

Measure a complete tiny restore into a new directory.

What to check: The timed extraction and byte comparison demonstrate a small local restore. Production RTO includes provisioning and application verification; RPO concerns the age of recoverable data.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.4 RPO and RTO

12. 21.5 tar

tar groups files into an archive. Compression is a separate transformation commonly selected through an option or pipeline. GNU tar can preserve additional metadata with explicit options, but a portable archive and a complete Linux-system backup are different goals.

This captures the named tree as relative paths and lists the archive afterward. Reading protected files requires appropriate permission. ACLs, extended attributes, SELinux context handling, ownership restoration, and sparse-file behavior need a deliberate policy rather than an assumption that -a or compression covers everything. (R50)

Never extract an untrusted archive as root into /. Inspect members and restore into a new, controlled directory first. An archive can contain surprising paths, links, or metadata. A live, changing directory may produce an inconsistent application state even when an archive file is created.

Linux example — 21.5

Create and list an archive of a file you control.

What to check: A relative archived path avoids restoring into an unintended absolute location.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.5 tar

15. 21.6 rsync

rsync synchronizes selected files between locations. Its archive option, -a, preserves a useful set of attributes but does not automatically include every metadata class, such as ACLs and extended attributes. Select -A, -X, or hard-link preservation when required and supported at both ends.

Here -n is a dry run and the source trailing slash means the directory’s contents. Review the exact source and destination before an actual transfer. --delete can propagate an erroneous empty source or mistaken target into destructive removal. Do not add it casually. (R49)

A mirrored directory is not automatically historical protection. Combine synchronization with verified version retention or a backup system appropriate to the failure model. Confirm that a remote or mounted destination is the intended storage before allowing a job to write.

Linux example — 21.6

Preview file-copy changes without deleting anything.

What to check: No files transfer during dry-run; review before executing the same command without --dry-run.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.6 rsync

18. 21.7 Filesystem Snapshots

A snapshot captures a filesystem or block-layer view at a point in time according to that technology’s semantics. It can shorten the interval during which an application must be quiesced and provide a stable source for a separate backup transfer.

Crash consistency means the captured state resembles a sudden interruption; it does not guarantee that every application has a meaningful transaction boundary. Application-consistent capture coordinates writes with the application or database. Multiple volumes can require coordinated capture to preserve relationships.

Snapshots that depend on the original pool do not survive loss of that pool. Monitor snapshot space and lifetime, and remove obsolete snapshots through the storage platform’s supported procedure. Leaving them indefinitely can create new capacity or performance risks while being mistaken for independent protection.

Linux example — 21.7

Inspect LVM snapshots if this host uses them.

What to check: Snapshot existence does not establish off-host recovery or database consistency.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.7 Filesystem Snapshots

20. 21.8 Database-Aware Backups

A database maintains relationships among data files, transaction logs, caches, and checkpoints. Copying its live directory without the database’s supported backup protocol can produce a set of files that never existed as one recoverable state.

For PostgreSQL, logical dumps, filesystem-level approaches with required conditions, and continuous archiving are distinct strategies. A per-database logical dump does not automatically capture every cluster-wide role or external dependency. Physical recovery can depend on compatible versions and the required write-ahead log. Select and test the method against the installed database documentation. (R51)

A restore drill should run queries that verify representative records and application invariants. Counting files or observing that a database process starts is not enough. Rehearse recovery into a new isolated instance rather than overwriting the healthy original to discover whether the backup works.

Linux example — 21.8

Create a logical PostgreSQL lab backup when that stack is configured.

What to check: Replace LAB_DATABASE with the approved lab database; a real test restores into a separate database and verifies queries.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.8 Database-Aware Backups

22. 21.9 Remote Backups

Remote storage adds a location boundary, but its credentials and administration determine how independent that boundary really is. A backup account should have only the operations the backup design requires. Prefer a separation that limits production’s ability to destroy retained recovery points.

Verify host identity when using SSH. Document network paths, bandwidth expectations, retry limits, and behavior during partial transfers. A job that runs longer than its schedule needs locking or another overlap policy; two concurrent jobs can compete for resources or confuse retention.

Monitor the age of the latest usable backup, not merely whether a process is running. Include destination capacity, transfer failures, and restore-read access. A remote repository that accepts new data but cannot be read under recovery credentials is not meeting the contract.

Linux example — 21.9

Preview backup delivery to an approved lab host.

What to check: Remote storage must be independently recoverable, protected, and monitored.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.9 Remote Backups

24. 21.10 Encryption

Encryption in transit protects data on the network; encryption at rest protects stored data under a particular key-management model. Neither compensates for a compromised endpoint that can legitimately decrypt the data.

Define where keys are generated, who can use them, how they are rotated, and how recovery obtains them when the source host is lost. A backup encrypted with a key stored only on that same host can be unrecoverable precisely when it is needed. A key copied unprotected beside the archive may add little meaningful protection.

Do not improvise a homegrown encryption format from command-line primitives for business backups. Use an approved tool with authenticated encryption, documented recovery, and a tested key escrow or recovery arrangement. Include access revocation and auditing in the design.

Linux example — 21.10

Encrypt a fresh sample file using a prompted symmetric passphrase.

What to check: Do not place a passphrase in the command; separately verify recovery and key custody.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.10 Encryption

26. 21.11 The 3-2-1 Strategy

The familiar 3-2-1 guideline calls for three copies, on two storage types or independent storage arrangements, with one copy off-site. It is a planning mnemonic, not a mathematical guarantee. Interpret independence according to actual failure domains rather than counting directory names.

A more detailed design can add offline or immutable retention and routine integrity validation. The point is to survive correlated failures: stolen credentials, controller loss, regional failure, or an unnoticed corrupt deployment. Three copies under one deletable account can share a single point of failure.

For HarborWorks, draw the production system, backup repository, separate retained copy, administrative identities, and encryption-key recovery path. Mark which failures affect each. Any untested boundary should remain an open readiness item rather than a reassuring checkmark.

Linux example — 21.11

Record separate copies and failure domains in a local worksheet.

What to check: Writing the plan does not create the copies; demonstrate restoration from the independent copy.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.11 The 3-2-1 Strategy

28. 21.12 Restore Testing

A restore test retrieves selected data into an isolated destination, checks integrity and metadata, starts the required software when applicable, and verifies business behavior. Record the recovery point, software versions, operator, elapsed time, exceptions, and cleanup.

Use known fixtures to make success observable: an expected file hash, a named database record, or a particular site release. Hash equality proves equality to the stored reference, not that the original content was correct. Combine integrity tests with application acceptance criteria.

Restore tests also test instructions. An operator who did not write the runbook should be able to find credentials and complete the steps. Record missing assumptions as defects and rerun the drill after correcting them.

Linux example — 21.12

Restore a controlled archive into a new directory.

What to check: Include permissions, required metadata, and application tests in larger recovery exercises.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.12 Restore Testing

30. 21.13 Bare-Metal Recovery

Bare-metal recovery rebuilds a usable machine after losing its original system environment. Required components can include firmware mode, partition layout, bootloader, filesystems, encryption unlocking, operating-system packages, network identity, configuration, and application data.

A raw image can simplify some restores but can also capture machine-specific state and age rapidly. Reproducible provisioning plus verified data restore can be more manageable for some fleets. Neither approach is universally superior; test the chosen method on representative replacement hardware or a new VM.

Do not clone host SSH keys, machine identities, or static addresses blindly into concurrently running systems. Recovery must distinguish restoring a replacement identity from introducing an additional machine. Keep network exposure restricted until this distinction is resolved.

Linux example — 21.13

Capture the storage and boot environment for recovery planning.

What to check: Rebuilding a bootable machine requires more than restoring application files.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.13 Bare-Metal Recovery

32. 21.14 Writing a Disaster-Recovery Plan

A useful plan names the incident authority, activation criteria, service priorities, dependencies, recovery objectives, required credentials, restoration sequence, validation, communication, and return-to-normal procedure. It also has an owner and a tested revision date.

Include decisions, not just commands. Who authorizes restoring an older recovery point? How will lost transactions be reconciled? What happens when the normal identity provider is unavailable? When does a failover become a permanent replacement rather than a temporary workaround?

Store a protected copy outside the system it describes. During a real incident, capture deviations and preserve evidence. Update the plan after the incident, but do not rewrite history to imply that an unplanned recovery was already documented.

Linux example — 21.14

Create a small recovery-plan worksheet.

What to check: Fill in concrete owners, steps, and measured results; keep credentials out of the worksheet.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — 21.14 Writing a Disaster-Recovery Plan

34. Requirement and simplest approach

Without root or network access, create a fixture, archive it, restore into a different directory, and compare its bytes. The tempting shortcut is to report success immediately after creating the archive. The missing proof is whether an operator can retrieve the expected content.

Run this exercise as an ordinary user. It operates only under a new private temporary directory and leaves that directory for inspection:

The manifest was created from the source before archiving. Verification is performed from the restored tree, so it does not accidentally check the original files. diff provides another view of content agreement. Expected hash checks report OK; actual results must be read on your machine.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Requirement and simplest approach

36. Show the limitation

Change the restored status.txt, then rerun the hash check. It should fail. Restore again into a third new directory from the trusted teaching archive and repeat the check. This proves that the test distinguishes known-good fixture bytes from modified bytes.

It does not prove off-site survival, encryption-key recovery, full metadata fidelity, database consistency, or bare-metal recovery. List those as separate tests in a real backup design. No single successful fixture should be marketed as all of disaster recovery.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Show the limitation

Change the restored status.txt, then rerun the hash check. It should fail. Restore again into a third new directory from the trusted teaching archive and repeat the check. This proves that the test distinguishes known-good fixture bytes from modified bytes.

It does not prove off-site survival, encryption-key recovery, full metadata fidelity, database consistency, or bare-metal recovery. List those as separate tests in a real backup design. No single successful fixture should be marketed as all of disaster recovery.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Show the limitation

38. Cleanup and production adaptation

Remove only the exact temporary tree after inspection; retain it while diagnosing a failed test. For HarborStatus, adapt the process to a protected destination, capture the relevant configuration and release identifier, restore on web2, apply correct ownership and labels, and verify the named HTTP response. Time the entire rebuild, not only extraction.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Cleanup and production adaptation

39. Practice and implementation lab

Write an RPO/RTO contract for the static site and one for a hypothetical order database. Explain why the same schedule and validation are unlikely to satisfy both. Ask a second person to use your restore instructions without additional verbal guidance.

Check your understanding. Is a snapshot necessarily an independent backup? No. Does an archive listing prove application recovery? No. Is the recovery key part of the recovery plan? Yes, under separate protection and access controls.

Chapter takeaway. A backup becomes dependable when its recovery boundary, integrity, and restoration procedure have been tested.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch023.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

40. Prove restored bytes match the source

Perform a real local archive and isolated restore, then compare content. This is not a complete disaster-recovery rehearsal. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Prove restored bytes match the source
